name: Nubians
info: The Nubians are a people indigenous to Nubia, the Nile valley from southern Egypt to northern Sudan, who speak Nubian languages, built the kingdoms of Kush and Christian Nubia, and live today in Egypt and Sudan.

facts.homeland: Nubia, from southern Egypt to northern Sudan; today Aswan Governorate in Egypt, especially Kom Ombo and Nasr al-Nuba, and Sudan’s Northern State from Wadi Halfa to al Dabbah near the Fourth Cataract, with many in Cairo and Khartoum; also the Midob and Birgid of Darfur and the Hill Nubians of Kordofan; ancient centres Kerma, Napata, Jebel Barkal and Meroë
facts.period: Neolithic settlements from 7000 BC; the A-Group (3700–2800 BC), C-Group (2300–1600 BC) and Kerma (2500–1500 BC) cultures; the Twenty-fifth Dynasty (744–656 BC); Napata and Meroë (to 300/350 AD); the Christian kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia (4th century to 1504); Islamization by the 16th century; displacement by the Aswan High Dam from the 1960s
facts.known: the Nubian languages, among them Nobiin and Old Nubian, written from the 8th century AD; archers famed in antiquity (“Land of the Bow”); the Twenty-fifth Dynasty that ruled all of Egypt; the pyramids of Jebel Barkal, Nuri, El Kerru and Meroë; the frescoes of Faras; the Baqt treaty; the Nubian vault; the Sebu birth ceremony
facts.sources: Egyptian texts, Greek authors such as Eratosthenes preserved in Strabo, Meroitic inscriptions and Greek inscriptions such as Silko’s at Kalabsha; Old Nubian documents; archaeology from Qustul to Kulubnarti; linguistic work by Claude Rilly, Julien Cooper and others; genetic studies of ancient and living Nubians

t: The Nubians are indigenous to the Nile valley between southern Egypt and northern Sudan, where Neolithic settlements date back to 7000 BC, and they speak Nilo-Saharan Nubian languages with Arabic as a second language.
Nubia was home to the Kerma culture, the Kingdom of Kush and the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, under which all of Egypt was united with Nubia from 744 to 656 BC.
The Aswan High Dam, built from the 1960s, flooded much of Lower Nubia and displaced 100,000 Nubians, many of them forcibly relocated to New Halfa, Khashm el Girba and “New Nubia” near Kom Ombo.
dyk: During the Yom Kippur War of 1973, Egypt used Nubians as code talkers.
ev: Neolithic settlements appear in central Nubia, with Wadi Halfa believed to be the oldest settlement of the central Nile valley
The Twenty-fifth Dynasty unites all of Egypt with Nubia
Eratosthenes records the Noubai west of the Nile as a numerous people divided into several kingdoms
The Kingdom of Kush disintegrates and gives way to Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia
Makuria repulses the Rashidun Caliphate’s invasion and the Baqt treaty is signed
Old Nubian is first attested in writing
Most Nubians have converted to Islam
The Aswan High Dam floods much of Lower Nubia and displaces about 100,000 Nubians

sections.origins:
The prehistory of Nubia goes back to the Paleolithic, around 300,000 years ago. Neolithic settlements in central Nubia date to 7000 BC, Wadi Halfa being believed the oldest in the central Nile valley, and by about 6000 BC its peoples farmed. Archaeologists divide its ancient history into the A-Group (3700–2800 BC), C-Group (2300–1600 BC) and Kerma (2500–1500 BC) cultures, followed by the age of the New Kingdom, Napata and Meroë. Biological studies show close affinities between the early Nubians and the predynastic peoples of southern Egypt, and Bruce Williams argued that Nubian elites took part with the early Egyptian rulers in shaping pharaonic civilisation.

The languages of early Nubia are debated. Peter Behrens and Marianne Bechhaus-Gerst suggested the C-Group and Kerma peoples spoke Berber and Cushitic languages; Claude Rilly and Julien Cooper argue that Kerma spoke an Eastern Sudanic language, while Cushitic was spoken in Lower Nubia. The first speakers of Nubian languages, another branch of Eastern Sudanic, came later.

The name comes from the Noba. Eratosthenes, in the 3rd century BC, described the Noubai as a numerous people west of the Nile; Rilly links the word to Meroitic nob, used for the people and for “slave”. By the 5th century AD the Noba used the name themselves.
sections.society:
Nubia had four kinds of land: the Nile valley in the north and centre, farmed by irrigation; western Sudan, with peasant farming and nomadism; eastern Sudan, mostly nomadic; and a fertile pastoral south where the larger farming communities lived. Kerma, Napata and Meroë were its largest towns in antiquity. Kings came from clans that controlled the gold mines, and Gamal Mokhtar noted that Nubians relied more than Upper Egyptians on mobile stock-raising.

Today the main Nile Nubian groups, from north to south, are the Kenzi, who speak Kenzi or Mattokki, the Faddicca, Halfawi, Sukkot and Mahas, who speak Nobiin, and the Danagla, who speak Andaandi. Most Nubians now work in the cities of Egypt and Sudan. Arabic, once learned mainly by men who travelled for work, is increasingly learned by women through school, radio and television, and more Nubian women work outside the home.

The Halfawis, Mahas and Danagla write with their own script and keep traditions such as Sebu, a ceremony for a birth. Scarification was once practised, three scars on each cheek among the Mahas and on the temples among the Danagla, but younger generations have abandoned it. Nubians share a common identity celebrated in poetry, novels, music and storytelling.
sections.beliefs:
Nubians today are Muslims, and their practice mixes Islam with traditional folk beliefs to some degree. In ancient times they followed a mixture of Kushite and Egyptian religion. Napata was a great religious centre: Jebel Barkal, a sandstone hill that its people saw as a rearing cobra, was declared by Egyptian priests to be the home of the god Amun, and Egyptian and Nubian gods were worshipped in Nubia for 2,500 years. Nubian kings and queens were buried in pyramids at Jebel Barkal, Nuri, El Kerru and Meroë.

After the fall of Kush, missionaries from Aksum and from Egypt competed in Nubia, and the Coptic Church established its authority. The kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia were Christian, and frescoes painted between 800 and 1200 at Faras and other cities show the religious life of their courts.

Islam arrived from the 8th century, first with Arab merchants. The Baqt treaty of 651 required the Nubians to keep a mosque for Muslim visitors. Conversion began with the elite and was carried mainly by Sufi preachers who settled in Nubia from the late 14th century; by the 16th century most Nubians were Muslims.
sections.arts:
The ancient Egyptians called Nubia tꜣ-stj, the “Land of the Bow”, and its warriors were famed for their skill with the bow and arrow. Nubian kings of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty were regarded as pious scholars and patrons of the arts, copying old Egyptian texts and restoring Egyptian practices, and their pyramids still stand at Jebel Barkal, Nuri, El Kerru and Meroë. Frank Yurco noted that royal crowns, Horus falcons and victory scenes were concentrated in Naqada Upper Egypt and the A-Group of Lower Nubia.

The Christian kingdoms wrote and painted in a style drawn from Byzantine Greek models. Greek served as a written language and lingua franca, taking words from Coptic and Nubian, and royal titles followed Byzantine models: an inscription names “the great King Moses [son] of Georgios, the King of the Nobatians, Alodia, Makuria”. The frescoes of Faras, painted between 800 and 1200, are in the Byzantine style. Old Nubian, written from the 8th century AD, may be the oldest well-recorded African language outside the Afroasiatic family.

Nubians invented the Nubian vault, a curved vaulted structure. Modern Nubian houses in Sudan have a large walled courtyard and an ornate gate, preferably facing the Nile, with bright stucco painted with family symbols, palm trees, geometric patterns or the evil eye.
sections.exchange:
Lower Nubia has been called “the corridor to Africa”, where Nubians met Egyptians, Greeks, Assyrians, Romans and Arabs. Ivory, animal skins and other goods of Africa passed through Nubia to Egypt, and Egyptian rulers sought its gold and trade routes, dominating Nubia in the New Kingdom. In turn Nubian rulers controlled Egypt for a century, and the Twenty-fifth Dynasty united Egypt with Nubia from 744 BC until the native Twenty-sixth Dynasty took Egypt back in 656 BC.

In the 4th century AD Kush disintegrated under worsening climate, rebellion and invasion by the Noba, while the Aksumites captured Meroë and looted its gold. In the Christian era the Rashidun Caliphate invaded Makuria in 651 and was repulsed twice, and the Baqt treaty that followed prevented further Arab invasions in exchange for 360 slaves a year. The Ottoman occupation of Lower Nubia in the 1560s and the Funj Sultanate’s annexation of the lands south of the Third Cataract by the early 16th century ended Christian Nubia.

Nubia then came under the Ottoman Empire, the Muhammad Ali dynasty and British colonial rule, and after Sudan’s independence in 1956 the Nubians were divided between Egypt and Sudan.
sections.legacy:
Nubians still live in the land of ancient Nubia, in Egypt and Sudan, and in the cities of both countries. The building of the Aswan High Dam from the 1960s flooded much of Lower Nubia, their ancestral land. It displaced 100,000 Nubians in Egypt and Sudan: an estimated 50,000 Halfawi Nubians were forcibly relocated from Wadi Halfa to Khashm el Girba and New Halfa in Sudan, and the Faddicca and Kenzi of Egypt were forcibly moved to villages of “New Nubia” near Kom Ombo.

Genetic studies find that Nubians cluster with the peoples of the Nile valley to the north and with their Afroasiatic-speaking neighbours, and that Christian-era Nubians of Kulubnarti already carried West Eurasian ancestry before the Arab migrations, reflecting long ties along the river.

The Nubian languages, among them Nobiin, Kenzi and Andaandi, are still spoken as mother tongues, and Nubian musicians such as Hamza El Din, Mohammed Wardi and Mohamed Mounir and writers such as Idris Ali carry the culture forward. Nubians have used their languages in public life too: in the Yom Kippur War of 1973 Egypt employed Nubian code talkers.

summary: The Nubians are the indigenous people of the Nile valley between southern Egypt and northern Sudan, heirs of Kerma, Kush and the Christian kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia. Muslims since the 16th century, they speak Nubian languages, and many were forcibly moved when the Aswan High Dam flooded much of Lower Nubia in the 1960s.
